Subject: Data incident escalation: cross-border consent & handover timing

Hi Markus,

We detected anomalous access flagged by our SIEM and are starting a coordinated review with our security ops team. Before we escalate, two quick asks so our legal/forensics teams are aligned with Redwood's obligations:

1) Please confirm Redwood's contractual notification windows and whether you treat an initial triage notice (high-level) as "notification" under your DPA, or if you consider the formal timeline to start when evidence is ready for transfer. We often see 24/72 hour calls in DPAs and want to align expectations.

2) Pinebridge is located in the EEA; if Redwood's forensics vendor needs to export data out of the EEA for deeper analysis, what consent paths do you require? Do you depend on written controller consent, or are there delegated subprocessor agreements that permit scoped transfers for forensic purposes?

3) Who will be Redwood's escalation owner for cross-border export approvals? We need a single point of contact and a playbook we can rely on (incl. timeline to approve/deny an export).

We will likely engage an external forensics provider (copied) to do a collection if needed. I attached our incident intake form and the standard Pinebridge consent checklist.

Thanks,
Sara Hartman
Sr. Security Program Manager
Pinebridge Health

Subject: Re: Data incident escalation: cross-border consent & handover timing

Sara — thanks for the heads up and for the intake form. High level answers below; follow-ups and a short call would help lock this down.

TL;DR: Redwood will send an initial triage notice within 24 hours of confirming an incident that impacts customer data. A formal notification that triggers contractual timelines will align to the DPA definition — typically when we have confirmed impacted dataset scope and evidence necessary for customer review. We propose the following practical escalation ownership and flows for Pinebridge:

- Ownership: Redwood Product Security (my team) owns triage and initial outreach; Legal (Kimberly/Monica) owns approval of any cross-border export or forensic vendor onboarding.
- Notification windows: initial triage email = within 24 hours; refined incident summary with scope and mitigation steps = within 72 hours where feasible. Formal "notification" per DPA will be the 72-hour scoped summary unless both parties agree otherwise.
- Forensics/export: Redwood will not export customer data out of the EEA unless one of these conditions is met: (a) Pinebridge provides documented written consent (email suffices) for the described export scope; (b) legal process (court/subpoena) compels export; (c) the data is pseudonymized to an extent agreed in advance and the vendor operates under a subprocessor agreement that includes SCC-like protections.

Proposed clause language you can pull into your DPA redline: 
"Forensics and Cross-Border Transfers: In the event of a security incident requiring forensic analysis, Processor shall: (i) notify Controller within 24 hours of triage confirmation; (ii) provide a scoped 72-hour incident summary with evidence required for Controller review; (iii) require Controller's documented consent prior to any export of Controller data outside the EEA for forensic analysis, except where export is compelled by lawful process; (iv) limit exported data to the minimum necessary and catalog chain-of-custody. Forensic vendors engaged by Processor will operate under contractual subprocessor terms with data handling and security measures at least equivalent to those in this DPA"

I'll attach a short 'consent-by-exception' flow diagram and a proposed forensic SLA (turnaround, access window, evidence retention). Can everyone confirm this is workable? If Pinebridge needs a shorter formal notification milestone we can discuss 48 vs 72 hours.

- Markus
Director, Product Security
Redwood Inference

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>

Date: Mon, 10 Aug 2026 09:50:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Data incident escalation: cross-border consent & handover timing

Markus / Monica — quick legal note on the proposed flows: I like the pragmatic approach but want to clarify a couple of legal constraints and an alternative we should offer.

1) EEA transfers: Redwood cannot rely on internal pseudonymization as a blanket exception. For any export we should require either documented controller consent (as Markus suggested) or ensure the forensics vendor is contractually a subprocessor with SCCs/BCRs in place. For time-sensitive matters a pre-approved 'forensics subprocessor' clause in the DPA (with a limited scope and pre-agreed safeguards) can accelerate things to avoid a last-minute consent freeze.

2) Timeline language: Many customers push for 'notification triggers' meaning the contractual clock starts on discovery. We should be explicit: initial operational notice within 24 hours, but the contractual DPA notifications (which often have remediation obligations) should start when the Controller has had the scoped evidence to evaluate — call it the 72-hour summary by default. For customers who insist on a discovery-based trigger we can offer a 48-hour alternative in the SOW/DPA with higher support/monitoring commitments.

3) Evidence custody: add a short para requiring chain-of-custody logs and a narrow export manifest to be delivered with any cross-border package. Limit forensic access windows to a default 14-day analysis window (extendable by agreement) and require proof of secure deletion after the agreed retention. This reduces indefinite data exports.

I'll draft a redline for the DPA that includes: (a) pre-approved forensics subprocessor section; (b) consent-by-exception path; (c) export manifest & 14-day default analysis window; (d) expedited amendment process (48–72 hours) for emergency transfers.

Kimberly Park
Associate General Counsel, Privacy & Security
Redwood Inference
